section_summary: This section concludes a statistical study of Japanese industry and labour, using Nagoya and Aichi Prefecture to discuss small factories, productivity, trade associations, wages and working conditions. Two file notes and a 1936 Embassy despatch then address nationalist obstacles to Ford’s expansion near Yokohama. The final pages contain a 1938 Department of State summary and the beginning of a consular report on the effects of the China Incident on Osaka’s small and medium scale industries.

subfiles.title: Study of Japanese Industry and Labour Conditions, Illustrated by the Nagoya District
subfiles.about: An extended study argues that small scale industry, mechanisation, local industry clusters and family labour shaped Japan’s export competitiveness.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion compares small and large manufacturers, Nagoya’s production and port trade, and rising productivity through motor power, improved machinery and industrial associations. It presents extensive tables on wages, worker age and sex, welfare allowances, living costs, hours, union membership and employment. Its conclusion argues that Japan’s relatively low money wages must be understood in the context of family income and young female labour, and rejects claims that export growth depends on social dumping.

subfiles.title: Nationalist Tendencies in Japanese Industry
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports that army influence has obstructed Ford’s purchase of land for a Japanese plant expansion.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses a staff interview with Ford’s plant manager and says the stalled expansion and an abandoned General Motors project illustrate hostility toward foreign controlled enterprises.

subfiles.title: Conversation with the Manager of Ford Motor Company, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Ford’s Yokohama manager describes blocked land purchases and options for expanding the company’s plant.
subfiles.summary: The manager says Yokohama declined to sell additional land and that an army objection stopped a second purchase. He prefers to wait rather than seek Embassy intervention or sue, and says Ford could add floors to its existing plant if needed.

subfiles.title: Summary of Osaka Report on the Effect of the China Incident
subfiles.about: A Department summary identifies raw material shortages as the chief problem reported by Osaka’s smaller industries.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the April 2 Osaka report and links reduced imports and priority for war industries to shortages, rising export prices and falling sales abroad.

subfiles.title: The Effect of the China Incident on the Small and Medium-Scale Industries of Osaka
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, American Vice Consul, Osaka
subfiles.about: A consular report summarizes Osaka industrialists’ accounts of shortages, government controls and declining exports during the China Incident.
subfiles.summary: Emmerson summarizes a March 4, 1938 Osaka newspaper round table, explicitly presenting participants’ statements as evidence of industrial attitudes rather than verified findings. General complaints concern scarce raw materials, export losses, taxation, skilled labour shortages and government controls that smaller firms consider unfair. The pages provided then discuss bicycles, machine tools and castings, glass, rubber goods, knitted goods and celluloid, before beginning the brush industry section. The report continues beyond page 119.
